articles.title: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
articles.summary: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
body: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.
Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.

"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."
Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.
Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled "Our Founders' Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump," which was published in 2020.
He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren.
His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

articles.title: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
articles.summary: As the fast-moving outbreak continues to spread in eastern Congo, fighting between rebels and the army is disrupting efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
body: BUNIA, Congo — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

articles.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
articles.summary: Leader Kim Jong Un reportedly visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons to cope with threats from the U.S. and South Korea.
body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.
Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.
KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

Trump still hopes to meet KimTrump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

articles.title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel. And, FCC violated ABC's free speech, judge says
articles.summary: The East Coast's weather is a major concern this holiday, as it could lead to coastal flooding. And, the judge says the FCC can't punish ABC for satire Trump doesn't like.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Severe storms sweeping across the nation threaten to cause widespread travel delays today, as millions of people gather with their loved ones. New York City officials announced that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled to Saturday due to the threat of powerful wind gusts that could reach up to 60 mph. This year marked the 100th procession, and the first time the iconic event is being postponed.

The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs targeting goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. Administration officials argue the measures counter unfair foreign trade practices, though critics question their ultimate effectiveness. Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.

Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in Eastern Iowa for lead contamination after the U.S. Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown yesterday. Officials said the controlled explosion was the only safe way to dispose of the bomb-making compound.

A federal judge has blocked Trump from challenging the ABC television network's broadcast licenses. U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan ruled that the president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional. AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction yesterday and dismissed the administration's request to throw out ABC and Disney's lawsuit challenging the review of the local license. Licenses typically last eight years and are rarely revoked. AliKhan's decision drew heavily on Trump's public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, as well as comments from Brendan Carr, the president's pick for chair of the Federal Communications Commission.

Holiday shopping season is in full swing. Before you spend, consider if you actually need what's in your cart. Sales are exciting because our brains are wired to seek newness. Retailers capitalize on that urge. To escape the cycle of constantly wanting more, shop intentionally and appreciate what you already own, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New. He shares his insights on breaking this cycle and finding joy in your current possessions with Life Kit.

For more guidance on how to reclaim joy without seeking newness, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Apple farmers across the Pacific Northwest are ripping out thousands of acres of orchards and grinding trees into mulch because growing the fruit no longer pays. Many say they're being crushed by soaring labor and equipment costs and international tariffs. Even multigenerational growers are leaving land unused rather than hemorrhaging money. Thousands of acres of fruit have been left to rot unpicked on branches, pushing some well-established farms into bankruptcy. Federal farm relief has also largely failed to reach specialty-crop growers. Take a look at photos and videos of affected farms, and read more about how the region that supplies the majority of the U.S.' fresh apples is handling the challenge.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

articles.title: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
articles.summary: The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.
body: Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.
That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.
The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.
Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."
When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.
"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.
Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.
"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."
The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.
"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."
(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."
Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.
"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

articles.title: Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.
articles.summary: Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius to prepare to dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide. And, after a nearly two-year legal battle, Kilmar Abrego Garcia's has voluntarily left the U.S.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.

Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.

NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.
There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here.

If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.

articles.title: Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief
articles.summary: "The public is rightly concerned," says the Republican lawmaker, who wants to know what the FBI and CIA knew about potential national security threats and whether Jensen Huang was warned.
body: Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled.

U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing.

There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.

Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached.

Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week.

For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats.
"What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked.
Huang's reinstatement, Fitzpatrick said, should not put those questions to rest.
"The public is rightly concerned, and they deserve answers," he said.

Fitzpatrick also wants to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche, who on Tuesday described Nvidia as a good corporate citizen, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department faces questions over Nvidia's chip exports to China.
"Anytime you do an investigation, you follow the facts wherever they lead, and you report those facts with unimpeachable integrity," Fitzpatrick said. "You leave no stone unturned."
The debate over Huang's reinstatement extends beyond Washington.
In Silicon Valley, his return has alarmed women and advocates who have spent years pushing for a better workplace culture, renewing questions about the limits of executive accountability.

articles.title: Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
articles.summary: Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts — from beating sun to freezing nights, fire and snow.
body: As dawn broke one recent morning over camp, we got one of our first full views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, normally hidden behind clouds.

Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts. The beating sun bakes you during the day, walking so close to the equator, but the nights quickly dip below freezing. Snow remains constantly in sight from humid rainforest and alpine landscapes, freshly charred from a wildfire three weeks before. And always beckoning is the peak, within sight, but seemingly never nearer; the high altitude means hikers need to walk slowly or else risk exhaustion and altitude sickness.

A group of friends and fellow hikers and I spent days camping at altitude to acclimatize before a final summit push during our second-to-last evening on the mountain. We trudged through heavy snow under the stars, cresting a massive volcanic crater rim, and leaned against drifts of what had become a full blizzard to reach the top in the early morning hours. I stood on the peak I'd seen only from a distance for the last week but saw only whiteness: all snow and ice, the absence of life and color heightened by my low oxygen levels.

Days later, having descended and decompressed and readying myself to fly back home, I looked back at the mountain one last time. For a few minutes, in the dusk light, the clouds parted and she revealed herself before disappearing again into the darkening evening, still as elusive as ever.

articles.title: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
articles.summary: The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
body: BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.
A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.
The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.

The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.

"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."

The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.
"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."

Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.

The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.
Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

articles.title: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is "strange" Trump has described Vladimir Putin as a friend.
body: Watch: Zelensky questions "strange'" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

articles.title: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing brief suspension of flights at airport
articles.summary: The brief ground stop came on the eve of the US Thanksgiving holiday, one of the busiest travel days of the year.
body: FedEx aircraft FedEx plane sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway dirt in the air while overshooting Miami runway
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) temporarily halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.

Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights resumed again about 90 minutes later.
The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.
The ground stop came on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.
Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.
At 21:41 local time, the FAA confirmed that "flights will be resuming shortly".
Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.
"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.
The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.
The Miami-Dade area is also under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.
A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
articles.summary: Pennsylvania and neighbouring states remain badly affected on Friday after both coasts were lashed with wind and rain.
body: Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits the US
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.

Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.
Conditions are forecast now to improve, though the National Weather Service (NWS) cautions that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms.
Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.
More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.
One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.
The number of homes reporting power cuts peaked at close to a million on Thursday evening - with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey badly affected.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. In Maryland, almost two million customers were asked by authorities to limit their water consumption to essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
Parts of eastern states are under states of emergency, including New York. Organisers of New York City's annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have also postponed the iconic event to Saturday.
Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather
On the West Coast, the concern was for exceptionally high tides and the associated risk of flooding.
Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft (2.4m) earlier this week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.
Watch: Man and dog narrowly escape powerful king tide in Oregon
Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.
Dramatic footage from Oregon showed a man and a dog being swept into the sea by a fierce, so-called king tide - but both escaped unharmed, police said.
FedEx aircraft FedEx plane sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway dirt in the air while overshooting Miami runway
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.

A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing". No injuries were reported, and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is investigating what happened.
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.

articles.title: Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
articles.summary: The struggle many face in buying a home has been the biggest issue of a bitter campaign.
body: Jangling keys has turned into a symbol of protest against Spain's housing struggles
Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.
Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.

The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.
The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace Sánchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.
The PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the Vox party which is polling in third place.
If Vox do win a share of power at a national level, it would be the first time for the far right in Spain's 50 years of democracy since Francisco Franco's dictatorship.
Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.
Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.
Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.
Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake

Sparking the protests in September was the eviction – and subsequent death in hospital – of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to Santiago). She could not afford a tripling of her rent in Madrid.
But it is Spain's third city, Valencia, that is at the heart of what many call a full-blown housing crisis.
"We want to live together but we look at the prices of property and it's impossible," says 25-year-old Nuria Cifuentes from the city.
She and her boyfriend Miguel Martínez work as sports journalists but are still living with their respective families because of the high cost of renting a flat, even with their combined salaries.
Nuria and Miguel want to live together but feel they are priced out
"Half of what we earn would go on rent of more than €1,000 a month," Miguel, 26, says.
We meet the couple outside Valencia's futuristic science museum, whose distinctive design is often compared to the skeleton of a whale.
This coastal location has witnessed the biggest rise in rent prices of any major Spanish city over the past half a decade, according to official data from the INE, the national statistics office.
One study from the city's Polytechnic University put the increase at 78% between 2020 and 2025.
Sánchez called a snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.

A revised version was later pushed through a parliamentary standing committee – restricting evictions and capping rent rises – but opponents say he has had eight years to sort the problem and has resolutely failed.
Nuria and Miguel say the soaring cost of housing means that life is on pause for them, as they're unable to make concrete plans for the future.
"Maybe we want to have kids, maybe we want to actually buy somewhere, but there are so many unknowns that all I see is a black expanse," Nuria says.
"The problem here is that our salaries are very low and life is very expensive."
The wider cost of living is the second most important issue for Spaniards, according to numerous surveys carried out during this election period.

Wages failing to catch up with rising prices – despite Spain's GDP growing faster than the three bigger EU countries, Germany, France and Italy – is another reason why Sánchez's PSOE party is only sitting in second place, according to final opinion polls.
Feijóo is said to be most likely to form the next government with the support of Vox under its leader Santiago Abascal.
Having called access to housing a "vital emergency", Feijóo wants to cut taxes for under-40s buying their first home and scrap the Socialists' housing law.
Pedro Sánchez (left) and Núñez Feijóo on screen during the leaders' debate
On housing, Vox has gone further than PSOE and PP, promising to prioritise Spaniards over foreigners for social housing and housing aid, as well as other welfare benefits.

On immigration, identified as the third most important issue, Vox advocates deportations for criminals from abroad and, most controversially, a policy of remigration for foreign nationals who "do not contribute to Spain".
Daniel, 30, is unemployed and says he is ready to vote for Vox for the first time
Opponents of Vox say those who have arrived legally and live and work peacefully risk being forced out.
But 30-year-old Daniel, who is currently unemployed, says he is ready to give his vote to Vox for the first time.
"First of all, it's immigration. It's bad in Spain today – that's why I'm going further to the right," he says.
"The left helps those who don't work, but we need people who work and contribute. We need to give less aid to people who come from abroad and don't contribute."
Daniel says taxes need to come down immediately.
"We are almost being charged to just breathe at the moment," he says.
We meet Daniel coming out of a shopping centre. We explain that other people we met in the previous hour who told us they support Vox did not want to give their name or be photographed.
Is he proud to be voting far right, or does he have concerns about his choice?
"I'll say it like it is… I've always been centre right but have gone to the extreme right… I've decided to choose nationalism."
Spain's control of its borders was criticised by 22 of its 26 EU partners in the summer, in a rebuke to Sánchez.
In July more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in just two days.
Sánchez has argued the foreign workforce is essential to Spain's economic growth, and in April announced plans to give half a million undocumented migrants legal status.
Maria and German feel they have little choice but to back the Socialist party

In the final days of the campaign, Sánchez has made a flurry of new spending announcements amounting to billions of euros, promising wage rises in the public sector, higher pensions and discounted transport.
Twenty-year-old student María García says she welcomes the promises but asks why they have come so late in the day.

"The Socialist party have been in power for eight years and now suddenly, during the election campaign, they are passing a lot of progressive laws – which I agree with – but isn't that hypocritical?" she says.
"I don't really have a choice but to vote for them, but come on – you had eight years to do all this!"
Maria's sentiments chime with those of her boyfriend German Martinez, 18.
I put it to them that nearly a fifth of Spaniards are said to be choosing Vox and a number of studies say it's set to be the top choice of first-time voters.
"I believe Spain is stepping into the lion's den because we are scared of the dogs outside. We need to be careful," she says.
"People need to inform themselves – just listen to what these guys say. That 20% of Spanish people agree with them really scares me."
Sánchez will be hoping that fear among the undecided of a national government that includes Vox will save him.
He is a great political survivor, but even if his party wins the most votes he has no obvious path to build a majority.
The man who called a snap election over housing now faces his own eviction - from office.

articles.title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
articles.summary: The contents of an eight-page letter by Gianni De Gennaro have been revealed days after his body was found at his Tuscany home.
body: Gianni De Gennaro worked in the anti-mafia directorate and became police chief before he headed Italian defence company Finmeccanica, later renamed Leonardo
Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.
His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.
In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.
The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.
But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.
In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.
The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.

"In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland."
Gianni De Gennaro (L) and anti-mafia judge Giovanni Falcone in 1992
"I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.
The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged issue in Italy.
The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.
On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she had been "deeply shocked" by the case.
"His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.
The letter was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.

According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.
The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres".
Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.

articles.title: Ex-media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
articles.summary: The former Murdoch media executive was overheard at an event referring to the way Grace Tame was dressed.
body: Tame says her "whole body was prickling with distress" over what Handbury said.
An Australian media mogul has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.

Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.

"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"

From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.
"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.
"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."

articles.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson launches last-ditch High Court appeal
articles.summary: Erin Patterson is serving life in prison for poisoning her relatives with a toxic mushroom lunch in 2023.
body: Patterson was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives
Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.
Erin Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.

Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".
She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.
Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.
She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.
Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.
He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.
She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.
Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

articles.title: Venezuela to scrap law that bars opposition from public office
articles.summary: The legislation has been criticised for enabling political persecution since it was introduced two years ago.
body: Jorge Rodríguez said no politician had been subjected to the law's provisions
Venezuela will repeal a law that bars opposition figures from assuming public office, the speaker of the National Assembly Jorge Rodríguez has said.
The legislation, which was introduced two years ago, has been criticised for enabling political persecution, but Rodríguez said no politician had been subjected to its provisions.
The older brother of Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodríguez said he expected the reforms to be approved next week.
Delcy Rodríguez's interim government has been negotiating with opposition parties since taking over at the start of the year, when former President Nicolás Maduro was seized by the United States.
The legislation, known as the Simón Bolívar Law, was passed shortly after the election in July 2024 in which then-incumbent Maduro was declared the winner amid widespread allegations of fraud.
Under the legislation, individuals who requested or supported foreign sanctions against Venezuela were permanently banned from political office and had their assets confiscated.
"Legislative processes are dynamic processes. That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through," Jorge Rodríguez said.

During subsequent talks, which began in August, the interim government and parts of the opposition agreed to review several other laws as part of a "route map towards democracy", according to an opposition statement.
Delcy Rodríguez has promised that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election despite being excluded from transition talks.
Machado returned to the country in October after more than 10 months in exile.
In the 2024 election, Machado's ally Edmundo González ran in her place after she was barred from running for office by Maduro's government.
The electoral authority, which was closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.
The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
articles.summary: The announcement comes a year after a military coup with its leaders promising a return to civilian rule within 12 months.
body: Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam said the postponement was driven by factors including final reasons
Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.
Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.
The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.
In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.
It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.
The presidency also reiterated its commitment to holding the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date for the vote.
Gen N'Tam was sworn in as transitional president a day after the military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embaló in November 2025.
The coup took place three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due to be announced.
Both Embaló and his main challenger, Fernando Dias, had claimed victory.
Embaló, who has since been living in exile in Morocco, was barred from returning to Guinea-Bissau last month, despite expressing an interest in contesting the elections.
Guinea-Bissau has experienced several coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974.

articles.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
articles.summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.
body: Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape

Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage
Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict
India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".
India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it
India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

articles.title: Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row
articles.summary: The Ugandan army is helping the Congolese military fight an Islamist militant group in the east of the country.
body: The planned withdrawal will end Uganda's nearly two-year campaign against ADF militants in Lubero
Uganda has announced plans to withdraw its troops from a town in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo within two weeks, as diplomatic tensions escalate between the two neighbours.
The troops will hand over security in Lubero, in North Kivu province, to Congolese forces after nearly two years of military operations, the Ugandan army said in a statement on Friday.

The announcement comes days after DR Congo summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over controversial social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is the son of President Yoweri Museveni.
The Ugandan military did not give a reason for the withdrawal or say whether it was linked to the diplomatic row.
What are Ugandan forces doing in DR Congo?

The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) were deployed to Lubero to pursue fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) Islamist group fleeing joint military operations elsewhere in eastern DR Congo.
The ADF, which originated in Uganda in the 1990s, is affiliated to the Islamic State and has been blamed for numerous deadly attacks on civilians in both countries.
Uganda first deployed troops to eastern DR Congo under the current joint military campaign in November 2021, following a series of bomb attacks in the Ugandan capital, Kampala.
Ugandan army spokesperson Col Chris Magezi said that the joint military campaign, known as Operation Shujaa, would continue elsewhere in DR Congo.
The planned withdrawal applies only to Lubero town.

Five years into the joint offensive, the ADF remains DR Congo's deadliest armed group, despite a significant decline in its activities in Uganda, according to the conflict monitoring organisation Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (Acled).
John Ngono, Acled's DR Congo analyst, said the group was killing an average of four civilians a day and had expanded into previously unaffected parts of eastern DR Congo.
He said the findings suggested that "Operation Shujaa may have improved security in Uganda while shifting the geographical impact of violence within the DRC".

Acled says the group has not carried out an attack in Uganda since June 2025, but its growing interest in mineral resources in DR Congo could help finance its operations and sustain its ability to threaten both countries.
The planned withdrawal comes amid strained relations between Uganda and DR Congo, despite years of close military co-operation.

Earlier this week, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to endorse a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo, threatening that Ugandan troops would seize it themselves if the rebels failed to do so.
The Congolese foreign ministry described his remarks as "particularly serious" and demanded that Uganda clarify its official position and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Gen Kainerugaba also defended Uganda's military presence in eastern DR Congo, insisting it was driven by security concerns.
The planned withdrawal comes amid renewed fighting between Congolese forces and rebels in the wider Lubero territory, raising fresh concerns about the safety of civilians.
Eastern DR Congo has endured decades of conflict involving dozens of armed groups, with millions of people forced to flee their homes.

articles.title: India busts cyberfraud and trafficking network rescuing 164 foreigners
articles.summary: Lured by IT job promises, the victims were allegedly forced into cybercrime, police say.
body: Noida, a suburb of Delhi, is a major IT and business hub
Police in India say they have uncovered an international cyberfraud and human trafficking operation on the outskirts of capital city Delhi and rescued 92 Indonesian and 72 Malaysian nationals.
They were allegedly lured to India with promises of lucrative IT jobs, but forced into cyber crime, according to police.
Police say the scheme was exposed after a Malaysian worker managed to escape and revealed the operation.

Dozens of foreign nationals have alleged that once they arrived in India, their passports were confiscated and they were held against their will in Noida - a Delhi suburb that is a major IT and business hub in northern India and home to several call centres.
Instead of the jobs and high salaries promised, police say, they were forced to pose as women online to lure unsuspecting victims into fake investment platforms.
So far one Malaysian national has been arrested in connection with the crime, and nearly 550 desktop computers, laptops and mobile phones have been confiscated, police say.
An investigation has now been launched into a potential wider global cyberfraud network.
Police and Indian banks have been trying to contend with an alarming rise in cyber fraud operations in recent years.
A paper, external by the Reserve Bank of India warned against rising digital fraud and "the manipulation of users through social engineering, coercion, or impersonation".

Figures from India's National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal show 2.8 million cyber fraud complaints were recorded in 2025, with losses of about 22,495 crore rupees, external ($2.42bn; £1.85 bn). It's a dramatic rise in complaints by more than 4,000% since 2021.
The federal government said most cases involved fake investment and trading scams.
In fake investment scams, fraudsters approach victims through social media, messaging groups or phone calls, posing as financial experts and promising high returns.

They lure victims to fake trading platforms that show fictitious profits. Some are allowed to withdraw small amounts to build trust, but when they try to cash out larger sums, they are blocked or asked to pay more. The fraudsters eventually disappear with their money.
The Noida case is the latest in a series of international cyberfraud call centres busted in north India in recent months, with police raids in Lucknow and Delhi's Pitampura area.

In July, Lucknow Police arrested 119 people after raiding a fake international call centre targeting US citizens. Employees allegedly posed as representatives of major companies and US government agencies to defraud victims.
