articles.title: EU leaders fail to bridge budget splits as talks stall
articles.summary: Aid for Ukraine was among the disputes as EU members hope to conclude talks by the end of the year.
body: Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to reduce EU spending
European Union (EU) leaders have deferred negotiations on its long-term budget after tensions surfaced over the bloc's spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.
Tense talks on the 2028-34 budget ended after 12 hours on Thursday at a summit in Brussels, with some members walking out of negotiations that will resume in December.

Divisions were largely split along the lines of countries, including France and Italy, wanting to approve a higher-spending proposal against those advocating for financial restraint, with Germany chief among them.
Many members want the budget locked in ahead of several high-stakes elections held across Europe in 2027, including in France.
Countries remain divided over a proposal to provide Ukraine with an additional loan of €45bn (£37.6bn), split between non-military and military funding.
Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary have objected to the loan, but German Chancellor Frederich Merz said uniform EU agreement was a condition for approving the broader budget.
"I stand by my view that aid for Ukraine must be supported by the European Union as a whole," Merz told reporters.
"The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Bulgaria, which previously opposed the plan, said it would agree to fund part of the loan that commits non-military financial support to Kyiv, marking a small sign of progress emerging from the special summit of the European Council.
EU members have been wrangling over the long-term budget after the European Commission submitted a €2tn proposal earlier this year, with some countries objecting to high levels of spending.
Those advocating higher spending want the funds to future-proof industries such as farming and invest in regional development. Fiscally cautious countries want to avoid amassing ballooning debt.
Thursday's talks were set up by the European Council to unblock the impasse, with a proposal to reduce spending by approximately €220bn to €230bn.
Under the current proposal, the budget totals €1.582tn, which includes €140bn to repay pandemic-era borrowing.
Four countries wanting to rein in the budget, including Denmark and Austria, walked out of negotiations after several hours of meetings.

Merz said there was "new movement" towards reducing the size of the EU budget, though he added "we are not there yet" when he confirmed that a new round of negotiations would not take place in Brussels on Friday.
European budgets requires approval from all 27 countries, with each country effectively holding veto power.
French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to lower long-term spending.

France's forthcoming presidential election came into focus during the EU budget talks, with frontrunner Marine Le Pen calling the talks an "underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people".
Last month, Le Pen announced she would significantly reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if she were to win the presidency.

Macron addressed Le Pen's remarks on the sidelines of the Brussels summit, saying: "It is an odd kind of arrogance to behave as if she is already in charge of France's destiny because, as things stand, she has not been elected."
Once the talks concluded, the European Council announced a two-day summit on 17 and 18 December would revive budget negotiations.
Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos was also named as the next President of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde from February 2027.

articles.title: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
articles.summary: The right-leaning ruling bloc led by the National Party has fallen short of the majority needed to govern.
body: If the ruling bloc cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.

Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. The party's leader Qiulae Wong has previously said she will negotiate first with the party that secures the largest number of seats.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.
In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.
"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.
A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.
Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.
'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years

articles.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
articles.summary: Nearly a third of crossings in early 2026 allegedly involved boats or engines from the German man's firm.
body: Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.
Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.
Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.
Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.
A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled)
At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.
There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.
In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."
It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.
French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.
The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.
While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".
Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.
In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.
In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.
Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.
News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.
He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.
One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cans
The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.
The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.
Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.
The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.
"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."
Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.
Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.
Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.
On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.
The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.
Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police
Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.
Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.
The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.
We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules
When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.
He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.
It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.
Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.
The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.
Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.
The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
articles.summary: A Paris appeals court rules Depardieu will go on trial for the alleged rape of Charlotte Arnould.
body: Gérard Depardieu has faced a series of allegations in recent years on film sets and elsewhere
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

articles.title: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
articles.summary: The possible environmental damage is still being assessed by Spain's sea rescue service.
body: The Med Emre vessel capsized near Ibiza and Spain's Clara Campoamor, a pollution control vessel, was sent to assess the environmental impact
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.

The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had been originally reported. The vessel remains, however, partially submerged.

That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface".
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

articles.title: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
articles.summary: Rebecca Taylor had been imprisoned in New Mexico for multiple theft and burglary charges.
body: A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.
The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.
She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.
Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.
The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.

The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.
"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.
All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.
However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.
The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

articles.title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
articles.summary: The pair were technicians for German company Rheinmetall, according to Italy's foreign ministry.
body: A Rheinmetall facility in Kuwait was targeted by Iran, Italian and Kuwaiti authorities said
Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.
The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.
Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi saying "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by its military.

Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.
It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.
Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.
The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.
Meanwhile, Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement: "An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working."

The two Italian nationals were working at an air defence detection station and performing maintenance work on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa, citing Italy's foreign ministry.
Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.
"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

articles.title: Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
articles.summary: Officials say the man confessed to travelling at speed and clipping the fuel truck as he was overtaking traffic.
body: Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.

The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.
Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.
Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.
The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".

"He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."

At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.
Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.

The raised motorway - a major artery for traffic around the Egyptian capital - was reopened by emergency services hours after the crash occurred, with the burnt-out wrecks of cars shifted to the side by bulldozers and diggers.

A cabinet minister said on Thursday that 10 million Egyptian pounds (£139,000; $182,000) had been donated to the families of the victims, while the nation's sports minister said all state-run celebratory activities would be cancelled in the aftermath of the crash.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years. Road collisions are also common, attributed to poor maintenance and violations of traffic laws, and leading to thousands of road deaths a year.

articles.title: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa
articles.summary: Lenacapavir, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection.
body: Lenacapavir has received WHO's approval for HIV prevention

Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.
Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.
The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.
The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.
Focus on Africa podcast: Lenacapavir offering new hope for HIV prevention?
Landmark deal paves way for cheaper HIV protection jab
Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.
In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.
Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025.
The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.

"These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.
More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.
The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.
It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.
South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.
Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.

The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.
The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

articles.title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling
articles.summary: A landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) convicted Myanmar of genocide against its Rohingya minority.
body: Myanmar's president Min Aung Hlaing has led the country since he seized power in a 2021 military coup

Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.
The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.
Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report.

"Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.
The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.
The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.
The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.
The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.
The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.
But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick.
While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.
More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders.

Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.
Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
articles.summary: The musician, who co-wrote some of the band's biggest hits, had been treated for prostate cancer.
body: Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023
Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the pop group Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.
Born in Tynemouth, he co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits, including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film; and also worked with artists like Robert Palmer, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.
In a statement, his bandmates said Taylor had fought "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer" and "passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23 November".
His wife, Tracey, said the musician "was the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day".
Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off
The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.
He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.
The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.
Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs
Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.
"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," said his bandmates Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (his bandmates were unrelated, despite sharing the same last name).
"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.

"Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time."
Sir Rod Stewart, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, paid tribute to his "dear pal".
"We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun," Sir Rod posted on Instagram.
Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse Macabre
Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.
Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.
They became so popular in the States that the press labeled them the leaders of a "Second British Invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.
During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.
Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and new wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980s
The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran, after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.
"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.
"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."
He went on to play on Robert Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.
After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.
In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.
When the group took the stage, singer Simon Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.
Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982
"Andy never took the easy musical route," said Le Bon in a personal statement marking his friend's death.
"His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.
"There's a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It'll never close up; I won't let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days."
Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982.
"For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first," she wrote in her statement.
"Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."
She continued: "Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life.
"The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful."

articles.title: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
articles.summary: Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as officials urged residents to leave the area.
body: Watch: Fire and smoke billows out of refinery owned by energy company Bangchak Corporation
Nine people have been injured after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, authorities have said.
Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.
A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).
The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.
Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.
An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.
Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.

On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.

It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

articles.title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
articles.summary: Despite the strikes, markets and restaurants in Riyadh remain busy as residents express trust in the government to protect them.
body: Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing number
Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.
"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".
Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.
One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.
Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.
He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.
He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.
"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."
The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.
According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.
Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.
In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.
Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.
As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.
Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.
Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.
As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.
The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.
Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.
The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.
Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal
Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.
But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.
Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.
We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.
Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.
"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."
Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.
The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November
The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.
Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.
The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.
Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer and Ahmed Nour

articles.title: Israeli justice system at tipping point as judges call for end to Netanyahu trial
articles.summary: Dropping of corruption charges against PM after highly unusual intervention could set damaging precedent
body: The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

“There were evidentiary difficulties in the case, but the position the judges laid out effectively means abandoning the media to the whims of politicians and publishers, and setting an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases,” said Yael Freidson, the legal correspondent for Haaretz, who has covered the trial since it began in 2020.
Related: ‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank

The judges urged prosecutors to drop one case because “the chances of a conviction are low”, seek a plea deal in a second, and reconsider the third set of charges. Even if prosecutors were to prove the allegations of fraud and breach of trust in that case, it was not clear that Netanyahu’s alleged behaviour amounted to criminal conduct, they said.

The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, who was summoned to court to hear the judges’ statement in person, must now decide whether to accept their recommendations and end a trial that has dominated and shaped Israeli politics for the best part of a decade.

The decision is not straightforward, even though the current bench has in effect signalled a not guilty verdict is a foregone conclusion. If the trial continues, their ruling could still be appealed to a higher court, where fresh judges could take a different stance.

“[The former prime minister] Ehud Olmert was acquitted on all charges by the district court and was subsequently convicted by the supreme court on a minor charge,” Ben Caspit wrote in Maariv. “It ain’t over till it’s over.”

“[Baharav-Miara] could opt to reach a lenient plea bargain agreement with the defendant and put it all to rest, but that would be an admission of the entire justice system’s failure and would further fuel the conspiracy theories that Netanyahu and his disciples have been pumping ever since he was indicted.”
Settling or dropping all charges would immediately and permanently absolve Netanyahu, ending the threat of jail time and dispelling the legal shadow hanging over his political future.
A bill making its way through the opposition-controlled parliament would in effect bar him from serving as prime minister until the trial is concluded.

Netanyahu, who has pleaded not guilty to all charges, claims he is the victim of a political witch-hunt and welcomed the judges’ recommendation as a vindication. “The truth has finally come to light,” he said.

Baharav-Miara has withstood pressure from the judges in the case twice before. In 2023 and in 2025 they urged prosecutors to drop bribery charges, the most serious ones that Netanyahu faces, although they stopped short of suggesting the whole trial should be wrapped up.

Perhaps the single point of agreement between Netanyahu’s supporters and his critics in relation to the trial is concern that it has been allowed to drag on for too long. Testimony from Netanyahu had extended over a year and a half, across 98 hearings, the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history, Freidson said. The transcripts from all the hearings run to more than 60,000 pages.

Oren Persico has sat in every hearing since the case began in 2020, covering the case for the investigative magazine The Seventh Eye. Over that period he watched the judges slowly lose control of their courtroom, he said.

“It started with giving the defence a lot of rope to do what they wanted. Netanyahu’s lawyer lashed out at the prosecution and humiliated them, almost every day, and attacked the judges, which should be an absolute red line in court,” he said. “I think the judges are afraid and tired; they just want to get it all over with.”

The sense of a bench cracking under pressure was exacerbated by the recommendation to reconsider charges in one of the cases against Netanyahu. These were laid out by prosecutors seven years ago, and have not changed since, prompting joking questions about whether the judges had even read the indictment, and serious ones about their political judgment.

When Netanyahu was indicted, he decided to fight the charges both inside and outside the courtroom, declaring war on the prosecution, the media, the police and key democratic and judicial institutions, Persico said.

“To keep himself out of jail, he tried to form an authoritarian state here in Israel, which tore apart society. I understand the interest in putting an end to that,” Persico said. “But ending the trial would send a terrible message to criminals and politicians and media bosses, that if you fight strongly enough you can get away with anything.”

articles.title: At critical juncture, Friedrich Merz finds Germans’ support for Ukraine wavering
articles.summary: German chancellor is on difficult terrain, at home and abroad, as he fights to maintain European backing for Kyiv
body: The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at home and abroad over his insistence that Europe must keep up support – both military and financial – for Ukraine.

At a Brussels summit on Thursday, Merz reiterated his view that all EU member states – pointedly, “not 23 or 24” – should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. He has threatened to veto the bloc’s budget unless all countries sign up to the loan, a stance that saw him accused of “classic blackmail” by Robert Fico, the populist prime minister of Slovakia. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria have also voiced their misgivings, to varying degrees, over Berlin’s dogged position.

But, unhappily for Merz, he cannot rely on the wholehearted support of the German public, either. A new survey released this week showed that, for the first time, Kyiv no longer enjoys majority support among the German population. The study by the Körber Foundation, showed 53% of those questioned were against Germany supporting Ukraine militarily, with only 46% in favour – compared with 59% just a year ago.

Merz, whose disapproval ratings stand at a record 88%, is therefore looking increasingly isolated. This all sends a worrying signal to Kyiv, which has counted on Germany as its biggest backer for some time, since Washington largely withdrew its favour.

The government’s attempts to push the case for Ukraine domestically now, when it is arguably most necessary, are not helped by the fact that German leaders have been reluctant to play up the support Germany has given to Kyiv since 2022 for fear of stoking embers of resentment.

This extends to keeping as quiet as possible about the estimated 1.33 million Ukrainians who have been given refuge in Germany since the full-scale invasion of their country, because of the strong tendency of the far-right, anti-immigrant Alternative für Deutschland to portray them as a burden.

As the cost of living crisis bites and the German public feels increasingly poorer economically, the debate over Ukraine funding is being framed – misleadingly, say critics – as a contest between the nation’s living standards and the billions paid to Ukraine’s defence.

This week Merz faced down opposition MPs in the Bundestag, the most vociferous from the pro-Kremlin AfD, who called for funding to Ukraine to be halted, as parliament debated the budget for 2027, Germany’s largest ever, due to be voted on by the weekend.

Opposition, however, is not only coming from the right. In Saxony-Anhalt, where in December the AfD may take over a state premiership for the first time, the BSW, a small, Russia-friendly, leftwing party, last month teamed up with the AfD to also demand a halt to arms supplies to Ukraine and the lifting of economic sanctions against Russia.
And on Thursday, an influential former Protestant church leader, pacifist and theologian, Margot Käßmann, called for a “change of course” and more diplomacy from the government.

“We must do everything we can to prevent war,” Käßmann said in an interview with DLF, a public broadcaster, insisting she would not bend to demands for Germans to defend themselves, instead calling for “much more diplomatic commitment”. She also accused Merz of not taking the “discomfort of the population seriously”.

Notably, the Körber survey found that the lowest support for Ukraine, 31%, was recorded in Germany’s eastern states, where the AfD – nationally five points ahead of Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance in the polls – has an increasing hold on power. Only 11% of east Germans are in favour of military help to Ukraine, while 75% would like to see a “normalisation” of relations with Russia, the survey found.
Merz now faces an uphill battle to win the German people round to his own government’s conviction that support for Ukraine is vital if Germany is to ensure its own security and future.

articles.title: Friday briefing: Will the proposed ban on conversion practices make it over the line?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: ​The draft bill currently being scrutinised by MPs faces a growing backlash, but nearly a decade after its proposal LGBTQ+ people are still waiting for protection
body: Good morning. There is broad consensus from LGBTQ+ advocates, mental health professionals and politicians that trying to change a person’s sexual orientation or gender identity against their will is abhorrent. For decades, campaigners have fought for a UK-wide ban on conversion practices, which can result in lasting trauma and alienation for victims.

Now, after years of delays, a ban finally looks within reach, with a draft bill currently being scrutinised by a committee of MPs and peers. But opposition has intensified in recent months from those who believe this could inadvertently criminalise parents, teachers and counsellors who ask questions about a young person’s gender identity. Meanwhile, campaigners argue there’s a world of difference between a sensitive discussion and abuse.
I spoke to our social affairs correspondent Jessica Murray about the developing row, but first the headlines.

UK politics | Labour’s internal divisions over the giant Rosebank oilfield have spilled into the open, with nearly 100 Labour MPs writing to the prime minister to express their opposition to the project.
Ukraine | EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year.

US news | Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.
UK news | A bill to implement the UK-EU deal will grant significant powers for ministers to enact even closer ties with Brussels, though it will stop short of Labour’s red lines.

Europe news | Gérard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial on a charge of raping a female actor at his Paris home in 2018, after an appeals ⁠court rejected his attempt to avoid having the case tried.

Jeanette Winterson’s powerful semi-autobiographical novel Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit draws on her experience of conversion practices, including violent exorcism, at the hands of her strict Pentecostal community in the north of England in the 1970s.

It’s tempting to view what was then described as “conversion therapy” through a historic lens, or associate it only with strict religious views. But conversion practices are far from a thing of the past: research by Stonewall last year found that 17% of LGBTQ+ Britons have experienced physical assault, 10% have experienced “exorcism” practices and 12% experienced “corrective rape” or sexual assault, all in an attempt to change their sexuality or gender identity.
When I asked Winterson about the proposed ban a few years ago, she told me: “Any country with equal rights should be banning conversion therapy. To me, it’s as bad as forced marriage.”
Eight years have passed since a ban on conversion practices was first pledged as part of Theresa May’s LGBT action plan, but fell apart amid moves to exclude trans people.

A similar commitment was included in Labour’s 2024 manifesto, but campaigners have become increasingly frustrated by the government’s reluctance to engage with the issue since the supreme court ruling on biological sex – which does not impact legally on a proposed ban.
The Scottish government also scrapped its plans to ban conversion practices via stand-alone Holyrood legislation, but will work with UK ministers on a UK-wide ban.

But in an interview with Jessica this week, the equalities minister Bridget Phillipson insisted Labour remains “committed” to the principle of the bill – in the face of growing criticism that the proposed bill could criminalise parents and healthcare professionals, or stifle free speech.

The draft bill, published in June, proposes the new offence should satisfy three elements: the intent to change an individual’s sexual orientation or gender identity, conduct that amounts to abuse, and that causes the victim serious harm. The third element in particular sets a pretty high bar for prosecution.

People found guilty of conversion practices would face up to five years in prison, an unlimited fine, or both. Courts would also be able to issue protection orders if someone is at risk of an abusive practice, including conduct outside England and Wales.

This happened to Shash Appan, who, at 16, was sent to stay with her grandparents in India after conflict with her family over her sexuality and gender identity. She was told the visit would last two weeks, but remained there for two years – during which time she was isolated, unable to travel alone and denied access to a phone or the internet.

“They wanted me to conform to what they saw as normal or natural,” Shash told Jessica. “They removed any form of gender expression. They would cut my hair, go through my belongings. I was only able to leave after convincing them to let me go and be homeless – they thought I’d come crawling back but I’ve stayed away since.”

Supporters argue that, while some elements of conversion practices, like physical assault, are already illegal, drawing them together under a blanket ban would give victims stronger legal protections as well as acting as a deterrent.

However, the bill has prompted criticism from some faith leaders. The Church of England, which has supported a ban on conversion practices relating to sexual orientation since 2017, says legislation must not “unintentionally criminalise providing appropriate prayer and pastoral care to those who seek it”, while the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales has called for the bill to be abandoned.

The gender-critical campaign group Sex Matters has also called for the bill to be withdrawn, arguing campaigners haven’t demonstrated a need for it and that it would cause “an immense amount of collateral damage.” Hilary Cass, the cross-bench peer and paediatrician who wrote a landmark review into young people’s gender services, also withdrew her support, claiming it was already having a “chilling effect” on healthcare professionals and their ability to conduct “appropriate and ethical therapy.”

Some campaigners supporting a ban are also worried that the framing of “abusive” practices suggests that some attempts at conversion are acceptable. Others want stronger safeguarding provisions, so that the burden does not fall on victims to come forward.
Will it criminalise parents or healthcare workers?

Much of the opposition to the bill relates to the inclusion of gender identity in the ban, and many of the voices ranged against it are those who oppose trans-inclusive single sex spaces – a position reinforced by last year’s supreme court ruling.

The Telegraph has also launched a campaign to scrap the draft bill, running articles claiming that supportive parents could be arrested under a ban, GPs would be at risk of sanction and that the scale of conversion practices is “vastly overestimated”.
And, separately, the Guardian has heard from parents worried that the proposals could make sensitive family interactions with counsellors or social workers much harder to navigate.

But Phillipson was adamant the ban will not affect ordinary parenting: “You can still have frank and open conversations with your children,” she told Jessica. “Even if you make it known you’re unhappy with your child’s orientation or gender identity, that’s not conversion.”

She describes some of the scenarios she’s come across where parents have crossed the line into abusive behaviour: “I’ve heard from people who had their hair forcibly cut off, or were threatened with corrective rape. That’s what the bill is trying to stop.”

Phillipson also stressed that therapists and counsellors will still be able to ask rigorous and exploratory questions. And the Ban Conversion Practices Coalition is keen that the final bill should include detailed notes to explain what is and isn’t covered, so the law can’t be undermined by vexatious complaints.

Prime minister Andy Burnham also reiterated his commitment to the ban earlier this week, albeit underlining the need for “very careful” pre-legislative scrutiny. Between the lines, Jessica says “they’re clearly leaving the door open for amendments and changes.”

The draft bill is only at the committee scrutiny stage and, as critical voices get louder and a growing number of Labour MPs put on record their opposition, “the backlash could get a lot bigger”, she predicts. Campaigners are broadly optimistic, but there’s still fear that, if it becomes more contentious, this government that is determinedly focused on easy wins and “breathing space” issues may back off. Does the long grass beckon?

This matters not only to those campaigning for an inclusive ban but to the wider community. For trans folk, it means yet another stressful public debate about whether they should be included in protections afforded to everyone else. But in recent years I’ve reported on the steady roll-back of rights across LGBTQ+ lives, in terms of safety, funding, and access to services. My sense is that this bill has come to mean more than the sum of its parts – a rare ray of hope for an embattled community.

articles.title: ‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank
articles.summary: Human rights groups report increasing attacks on Palestinian healthcare workers
body: Yousef Diriyeh and his son Hadi, both paramedics in the occupied West Bank, were lifting a wounded young woman into their ambulance when they heard shots crack and bullets whistle past their heads.

Less than an hour earlier, armed Israeli settlers had attacked the village of Qusra, killing three Palestinians and wounding several more. They were now shooting at the paramedics who had come to help.
Diriyeh urged his son to hurry as bullets struck the windscreen. It was the first time he and Hadi had come under attack.

As he sped to a hospital in Nablus, Diriyeh, now 50, remembers thinking to himself that the events of that day – 11 October 2023, shortly after Hamas launched the attack on Israel that triggered the Gaza war – would mark the beginning of a series of attacks on emergency responders such as him and his son.

Since 7 October 2023, Israeli soldiers and militant settlers have repeatedly attacked Palestinian paramedics and blocked them from reaching the wounded in the West Bank. Violence against healthcare workers rose by more than 350% between 2022 and 2024, according to Physicians for Human Rights Israel, a non-profit organisation which documents human rights abuse affecting the right to health in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Insecurity Insight, a Geneva-based nonprofit humanitarian research organisation, recorded 1,020 attacks on health workers in the region from 7 October 2023 to 15 September 2026.

Physicians for Human Rights Israel shared dozens of videos with the Guardian, including of the incident shown above in October 2023 in Huwara, showing militant Israeli settlers throwing stones at ambulances, using cars to block their passage, and, in some cases, shooting at them. The footage also shows damaged ambulances, bloodstains on drivers’ seats and injured paramedics. It does not include the attack on Diriyeh and his son, which was not filmed.
The Guardian joined a team of paramedics near Nablus and spent a day in their ambulance, with Diriyeh at the wheel as he recalled that moment.

“That day I realised the militant settlers had fired directly at us with the intent to kill,” said Diriyeh, a tall, broad man with a thick, greying beard, driving along Route 60 towards villages recently targetted by settlers.

Israel has retained effective control over the occupied West Bank, including its borders and the movement of people, despite the Palestinian Authority’s nominal autonomy. As an occupying power, Israel is obliged to keep civilian medical services running, yet Israeli forces and settlers systematically subject emergency workers to abuse and violence.

“Over the last two years, [attacks] have increased at an insane rate – meaning there are attacks taking place every single day,” said Diriyeh. He has been based for the last 15 years in Aqraba, a village near Nablus for the last 15 years. “Sometimes there might be three, five or even six separate attacks taking place simultaneously.”

Heading south from Nablus, the village of al-Sawiya comes into view.“It was near here that settlers killed my colleague and friend, Mohammed,” Diriyeh said, pointing towards the houses. Mohammed Awad Allah Musa, an ambulance driver for the Palestine Red Crescent Society, was killed on 21 April 2024 taking wounded Palestinians to hospital.
He was one of 13 West Bank health workers killed since 7 October 2023, according to Insecurity Insight.
In news reports of recent settler attacks, reports have regularly suggested that ambulances have been prevented from reaching injured people in the region.

Ambulance crews in the occupied West Bank depend on Israeli military approval, passing through checkpoints to reach patients and take them to hospital. By December 2025, the UN had recorded 925 obstacles in place in the occupied West Bank, including checkpoints, road gates and roadblocks.
Militant settlers have also obstructed ambulances, Diriyeh said.

“They try to prevent us from passing by driving very slowly in front of us. Sometimes, when a settler’s vehicle is ahead, I might attempt to overtake, only for another settler to block the way to stop me,” he said.

In some West Bank villages, militant settlers have locked the gates, leaving ambulances stuck at their stations and unable to answer emergency calls. Since first occupying the West Bank in 1967, Israeli forces have continued to install road gates at the entrances to some Palestinian villages.

“Sometimes they come and lock the gates in and out of Aqraba – you’d practically need a helicopter to get past them,” Diriyeh added. “Some women have even given birth inside the ambulance itself when these gates are blocked.”
Omar, a 34-year-old emergency medical worker from Nablus, told Physicians for Human Rights Israel that soldiers at a checkpoint in Awarta stopped an ambulance carrying a woman in labour.

“Traffic was backed up, and the soldiers were refusing to let anyone through,” he said. “By the time they finally let us through, there was even more traffic ahead. In the end, while we were still on the way, the woman gave birth.”

The Pulitzer prize-winning book A Day in the Life of Abed Salama follows a father’s search for his son after a school bus crash in 2012 near Jerusalem. The writer, Nathan Thrall, who is based in Jerusalem, said more than a decade later that restrictions on Palestinian movement in the West Bank had become far worse.

“For many, they are the most severe they have experienced since the occupation began,” he said. “The goal, as ever, is to constrict Palestinians into ever-tightening spaces so that their land may be taken over for Israeli settlement and de facto annexation, a project that is not only steadily succeeding but accelerating rapidly.”

Imran Anati, a researcher for Physicians for Human Rights Israel, said: “These are not isolated incidents, but a systematic assault on Palestinian emergency medical care for which Israel bears responsibility.”

The Israeli military denied allegations that it had obstructed the work of Palestinian paramedics or prevented them from reaching the wounded, saying it “enables freedom of movement for medical teams” throughout the Palestinian territory. It said it condemned all acts of violence against medical teams and ambulances.

Diriyeh’s job has become one of the most dangerous in the occupied West Bank, as settler attacks become ever more frequent. The Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism”, while the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, called the actions “ethnic cleansing”.
Diriyeh said he had made the “difficult decision” to ask his 20-year-old son to stop working with him.
He said on his first day of training as an ambulance driver in late 2013, the first case he had to handle involved a settler’s vehicle which had overturned on the road to Jericho.
He said Israeli emergency services couldn’t locate the vehicle, so Palestinian paramedics arrived and provided medical aid to the settlers on-site.

“In my career, I have provided medical aid to Israeli soldiers, too,” he said. “Whether they are Palestinian, Israeli, Christian, Muslim, Druze, or Jewish – it is of no concern to me. My mission is simply to provide humanitarian aid to anyone who needs it. That is my job.
“And it’s painful to think that today, a Palestinian life is worth less than an Israeli one.”
Additional reporting by Jamal Risheq.

articles.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
articles.summary: What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape
body: As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.
“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography.
