articles.summary: Public Committee Against Torture in Israel examined 42 complaints against Shin Bet interrogators over past decade
body: Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from Palestinian prisoners, sometimes documenting abuse in official records or granting advanced approval for “special measures” in interrogation, according to a report from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI).
This dangerous practice risked leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice, as Israel moved to implement a racist new death penalty law that targets Palestinians, the report said.
PCATI examined 42 cases in which Palestinians filed complaints about the use of torture by Shin Bet interrogators over the last decade.
More than three-quarters said they confessed after the use of “torture or other illegal methods”, and one in 10 provided incriminating statements about other people under torture.

“When it comes to Palestinian detainees, the Israeli legal system officially sanctions torture as a tool for extracting confessions, regardless of whether the content of those confessions is true,” said Sari Bashi, the executive director of PCATI.
“Torture as a tool of interrogation is particularly egregious given initiatives to impose the death penalty in Israel for the first time since 1962.”

Over the years, in hundreds of testimonies, Palestinian detainees have consistently described interrogations employing extreme sleep deprivation, physical violence such as slapping and kicking, threats, sexual violence and being held in stress positions.

Some of this abuse is also laid out in the official records of Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security service. PCATI details the case of a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019 who was subjected to extreme sleep deprivation.

During an interrogation period lasting 27.5 days, or 660 hours, he was questioned for more than 552 hours, an average of 20 hours a day, with one session lasting nearly 48 hours. Some of the remaining 108 hours were spent travelling to and attending detention hearings.

In a 1999 ruling, Israel’s supreme court explicitly prohibited sleep deprivation as a deliberate interrogation method. Despite this, the lawyer was convicted of involvement in shooting attacks based on information extracted during this period.
The state inspector for complaints about Shin Bet interrogations (Mavtan) ruled that the interrogations took place in accordance with procedures, PCATI said.
More than 1,680 torture complaints were filed between 2001 and 2024 with Mavtan. None have led to an indictment.
Other cases are indirectly documented in Israeli judicial records, although judges rarely accept testimony about torture of Palestinians, PCATI said.

In one case, a detainee’s false confession, made under torture, was used as evidence by prosecutors. The man was released after his lawyer presented proof that he was not present at the scene of the crime, PCATI said.
Sleep deprivation was the most frequently used form of torture in complaints examined by PCATI, but more than half included the use of stress positions and other forms of physical violence.

Israel is a signatory to the UN convention against torture, but its legal system has effectively codified the use of violence and abuse where it is deemed “necessary” to extract life-saving information, PCATI said.

In a “necessity interrogation” or “military interrogation”, Shin Bet officials torture detainees “after consulting with their superiors and following an internal procedure for documenting their decisions and conduct”, the report said.

“[A] supposedly narrow exception ballooned and developed into a sprawling system of legal and administrative exceptions that swallowed the so-called rule, enabling the use of violence while maintaining the appearance of prohibition,” it continued.

There is no publicly available information on the scale of “necessity interrogations” inside the Shin Bet, PCATI said. They are an urgent concern as Israel moves to end a de facto moratorium on the death penalty, which had stood since the 1962 execution of the Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann.

“The death penalty is always wrong, because it’s cruel, irreversible and negates the right to life. No one should be executed, particularly not in a system tainted by systematic violence,” Bashi said.
In March, the Knesset passed a racist law allowing the execution of Palestinians convicted of terror charges over deadly attacks, but not Jewish Israelis who commit similar crimes.
In the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians are tried in military courts, execution is now the default punishment for a defendant found guilty of deadly terror attacks.
The legislation drew fierce international criticism, including from the UN’s high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, who warned that it would constitute a war crime if enacted.
A separate law empowers a special tribunal to impose death sentences in cases arising from the 7 October 2023 attacks.
Even in rare cases where courts have excluded confessions obtained under torture, Israeli case law allows prosecutors to use information derived from them as evidence to secure convictions.

PCATI said that as detention conditions worsened after October 2023, rights groups documented a sharp rise in violence by Israeli prison guards and soldiers, including beatings, attacks with dogs, electric shocks, threats and rape.

At least 103 Palestinian detainees have died in Israeli custody since 7 October 2023. Of 10 postmortems reviewed by Physicians for Human Rights Israel, five showed signs of physical assault and six showed evidence of medical neglect.
The Israel Prison Service said “all prisoners are held in accordance with the law”. The Shin Bet and Israel’s justice ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Stop using teargas on battlefield, dozens of countries tell Russia
articles.summary: Call comes after chemical weapons watchdog confirms traces of riot-control agent found in trench hit with Russian grenade. What we know on day 1,737
body: Officials from 34 countries and the EU have called on Russia to stop using riot-control gas on the ⁠battlefield, after the global chemical weapons watchdog confirmed that Ukraine had found traces of teargas in a trench Kyiv said was hit with ⁠a Russian grenade. The joint statement was issued on Wednesday in response to a Ukrainian report circulated ​to 193 countries as the Organisation ‌for the Prohibition of Chemical ‌Weapons (OPCW) gathered in The Hague this week. Ukraine said it had documented more than 14,000 ‌cases of munitions filled with riot-control agents and toxic chemicals used by Russia on the frontline since 2022. The OPCW said laboratories approved by the watchdog had “confirmed the presence of a riot-control agent (CS)” in samples ​collected at the trench.

Riot-control agents such as CS, a form of teargas, are banned in warfare. “We call for the immediate cessation of the use of any toxic chemicals and of ⁠riot control agents as a method of warfare in Ukraine,” non-proliferation directors ​from Britain, France, Germany, Japan, ​New Zealand and the EU, among others, said in a statement. News reports midyear said western intelligence had found that Russian forces were using riot-control agents to drive Ukrainian troops out of trenches and into the open so they could fire on them. Russia has denied using illegal munitions, and has accused Ukraine of doing so.

At least five people ⁠were ⁠killed ​and three injured ⁠in a ⁠drone ​attack ‌on ‌a car ‌park in Vesioloye in the Russian-occupied part of ‌Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Russian-installed governor Yevgeny ​Balitsky said ​on Thursday. ​In Russia, debris from ⁠drones shot down over the ⁠Tuymazinsky district ⁠in ​the Bashkortostan region fell in an ⁠industrial zone and caused a fire, ⁠the head of ​the district ‌said.

Russian ⁠forces carried out a huge ⁠overnight strike on Ukraine, hitting ⁠military-industrial facilities in Kyiv, ​the ‌Interfax ‌news agency quoted the defence ministry as saying on Thursday. ​Late on Wednesday, Russian forces attacked the Ukrainian capital with ballistic ⁠missiles, striking a shopping centre and two other ⁠buildings, mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Three people were wounded, with one in a serious condition, he said, warning residents to ‌remain in shelters.

Ukrainian forces struck a major airbase in Russia, damaging ⁠five planes used to launch missiles and bombs at Ukraine, the Ukrainian general staff said. Russia ⁠did not immediately ⁠comment on ​Wednesday’s claim, which said the Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region had been hit in Kyiv’s latest long-range attack. Three MiG-31 jets and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were knocked out ​of operation “for some time”, the general ‌staff said.

German chancellor Friedrich Merz accused Russia of “escalating” threats to European security as he defended ⁠his government’s plans to ⁠bolster defence spending and maintain ​financial aid to Ukraine. Opposition parties, including on the far right and hard left, have called for an end to aid to Kyiv. “It ⁠cannot be said often enough, against the far right as much as the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine,” Merz told the Bundestag. “Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea; Russia is ​escalating in space, and Russia is by now also escalating ‌massively here in our own ‌country.”

US envoy Jared Kushner has warned against a downward spiral in the Ukraine conflict, which he called “a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia”. He told a German podcast that “it won’t take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively”. Kushner also appeared to accuse the Europeans of hypocrisy for continuing to buy Russian energy while backing Ukraine.

Poland will create a no-fly zone near the Ukrainian border, a deputy defence minister has announced, after several incursions into its airspace, which it blamed on Russia. The no-fly zone is intended to allow Polish forces to quickly identify any Russian military aircraft and shoot them down if necessary.

Preparations for Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian utility infrastructure this winter are a top priority for the government, a Russian deputy prime minister said. “This ‌is now the most important question: how we’ll get through the winter, especially given drone attacks, particularly in the border regions,” Marat Khusnullin told lawmakers on Wednesday.

Nine more Ukrainian children have been reunited with ⁠their families amid the war in Ukraine, bringing the total to 43, under an ⁠initiative led by ⁠US first ​lady Melania Trump, the White House and Russia said on Wednesday. There was no immediate comment from Ukrainian authorities.

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Why young people are having less sex than ever
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: A new study of sexual trends in Britain has found that one in three under-25s have never had sex, a flashy headline that obscures the real reasons behind a ‘sex recession’ among young people
body: Good morning. Let’s talk about sex! I know, I know; it’s not 9am yet. But trust me, you’ll enjoy it and I won’t ask you to do anything that puts your back out before your first brew.

The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, or Natsal, is a big-deal publication: a substantial piece of research capturing trends in British intimacy every decade since 1990. This week, it made more headlines than usual with the revelation that sex among adults of all genders and sexualities has slumped – and the standout finding that one in three under-25s report they have never had sexual intercourse.

What is driving this decline, does it matter and who’s going to contribute to my pension if we all stop having babies? (Not really, I’m doing a stand-alone newsletter on the last one.) To explore this further, I spoke to Guardian writer Aneesa Ahmed and Natsal researcher Luke Muschialli, both in their 20s. But first, the headlines.
Climate | For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned.
Ukraine | Britain will add to its multimillion pound investments in rebuilding Ukraine’s energy system by funding a windfarm project capable of powering 300,000 Ukrainian households.
UK news | Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk in “devastating news” for staff in the run-up to Christmas.

Gaza | A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

Trump tariffs | Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.

Back in the last century, when I began my dating life, everybody had a Number. Your Number was how many folk you’d had sex with on your search for The One. I remember this dubious social construct as an impossible balancing act – between proving I was desirable, experienced and up-for-it on the one hand, while also not sounding like a slag on the other. It was the 90s …
Fast-forward three decades, and I’m sitting in an office booth with my brilliant colleague Aneesa Ahmed who, at 26, tells me gently: “That’s not really a thing any more.”

“My generation was born into this sex positive, ‘woke’ era, where it’s bad to slut-shame women, though sadly it still happens. As for The One, decentering romantic partnership and monogamy is big among people my age”.

Attitudes to sex and identity have transformed between our generations. Largely for the better, in terms of more nuance around gender and consent, and sometimes for the worse, most obviously with the rise of the manosphere. But the Natsal study wasn’t the first to pinpoint a decline in physical intimacy among Aneesa’s peers, and I’m interested in the factors driving what is described as a “sex recession” among younger people.
Why are younger people having less sex?

There are multiple avenues worth exploring, says Aneesa, who reports regularly on gen Z attitudes to sex and relationships. “In the heterosexual context, women are much more independent, not looking for a husband to provide for them, and not willing to put up with some men who have horrible, misogynist opinions.” (I’ve written before about this ideological gender gap, with younger British men almost twice as likely to vote for Reform UK as their female peers.)

Meanwhile, young men find our templates of masculinity overwhelming or unappealing. Some believe the only way to approach women is to be an aggressive alpha, while others are anxious about making any move for fear of coming across as creepy. Either way, connection is lost.

There are also changes in the social dynamic that aren’t captured by raw data. Her peers are much more interested in “situationships”: many have never had a committed partner. They’re much less bound to a traditional linear progression towards a nuclear family – not that they can afford to start one. Nurturing friendships and platonic love has become more important than the idea of a fix-all romance.

The average age at which young people first have sex rose to 18 in the latest survey, up from 16 in 2010. For young people who grew up with much greater education about consent and boundaries, says Aneesa, “people don’t put up with disrespect.” And with growing numbers identifying as LGBTQ+ there’s less urge to rush into intimacy “with people that might not care or understand”.
What the survey doesn’t tell us

Back to Natsal. Luke Muschialli, a research assistant in epidemiology at University College London, worked on the survey. He’s 24, and wary of picking an instant culprit for the decline in sexual activity (eg, “They’re all on their phones!”).

I catch him after the initial tranche of “no sex please, we’re British/snowflakes/pick your own” headlines have been published. There’s a separate conversation to be had about why some older adults lose their minds at research like this: is it just prurience, angst about younger people’s capacity for intimacy in a digital-first world, confronting memories of how we behaved when we were that age?

Natsal cautions me that a lot of media reaction has drawn a causal link between the findings that online sexual behaviours such as sexting and porn use are high among young people, and that they are having less sex. “But our study is not able to show whether there’s a direct substitution for partnered sexual activity with online sexual behaviour, which should be the focus of future research.”

He’s also concerned that much of the reporting has glossed over the finding that low sexual wellbeing is very common among younger people. “My biggest worry is that people will look at the findings and think it’s a reason to disinvest in sexual and relationship health services. Young people are still really in need of STI and HIV support that can adapt to their changing behaviour.”
Is the poly-crisis stopping young people having sex?

Luke is foremost a researcher, rather than a representative of his entire generation. He’s keen to emphasise that Natsal can identify the trends but can’t explain why they are happening. Still, one obvious interpretation is positive: the data reflects young people who feel able to negotiate safe, wanted sexual encounters much more effectively.
But Luke’s hunch is that young people are also experiencing “a constrained opportunity for sex”.

“I wonder how my friends can face meeting new partners through the age-old tradition of a night out on the town, when their entry-level salaries can’t swing for an £8 pint or a staggeringly high nightclub entry fee,” Luke says. Apps can make introductions, but they don’t bring down the cost of your date. “Do our opportunities for sex decrease now that young people are living with their parents well into their 20s? I also wonder how a generation increasingly grappling with their own mental health have space for the human connection and necessary vulnerability that comes with sex and romance,” he says.

Back with Aneesa, I’m also curious about the substantial drop in the proportion of women wanting children, more than doubling from 8% to 17% over the past decade – an increase driven primarily by women under 35.

I’m well aware of the shift away from biological clock panic that dominated the media when I was in my 20s: is it about younger women giving up on that heteronormative progression, or recognising that child-rearing is expensive and exhausting, or having more role models of single childless women than Bridget Jones?

“This is very much a product of the society that we live in,” says Aneesa, citing the lack of support with childcare, for single mothers in particular. Also, she says, and this one hits home: “Seeing the women who came before us having to work full-time, and still taking on all the domestic labour … it’s off-putting.”

Longer-term consequences aside, Aneesa draws my focus back to the two in three under-25s who are sexually active. Gen Z are not prudes, as they’re typically branded when another survey like this pops up. But their pleasure-seeking happens in an evolving context.

“The idea that we’re an uptight generation is totally untrue,” she says. “Yes, we want these experiences, but in a safe, consensual way, with partners we can trust. And for us, that’s what is important now.”

articles.title: Welfare overhaul plans put rare focus on improving benefits system for disabled claimants
articles.summary: Timms review tackles some big questions about a flawed system – but leaves other issues in the ‘maybe later’ drawer
body: Stephen Timms would be forgiven for feeling his thunder has been stolen. The minister for social security has spent the last year reviewing personal independence payments (Pip) in light of Keir Starmer’s doomed measures last summer, but last week the Milburn review pitched a set of changes to the key disability benefit to great fanfare.
But when Timms took to the House of Commons to call for a “fundamental overhaul” of Pip on Tuesday, it was clear these were altogether bigger – and notably not explicitly cost-saving – ideas.

Whereas Milburn proposed £3.6bn in cuts to under-25s’ benefits, Timms offered disability campaigners something they have rarely come to expect from benefit changes: a focus not on shrinking the bill but on making the system better for claimants.

That means tackling the inaccuracy of assessments, particularly for those with fluctuating conditions, and “rehumanising” a process that has long been accused of harming disabled people’s mental and physical health.

The government has already accepted two ideas to this end: introducing a fast-track system that will relieve people with the most severe and easily evidenced conditions from going through an interview, and reducing award reviews for people whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve – something that will incense critics but win cheers from advocates who have campaigned against “pointless” reassessments since the coalition government phased out lifetime awards as part of Pip’s creation in 2013.

Much of the rest of Timms’s review could be filed in what you might call the “maybe later” drawer: several major but slightly vague changes to the Pip assessment and payments process that ministers will now need to decide whether they want to flesh out and implement.

One key idea is a new impact assessment designed to measure the actual costs that come with someone’s health conditions, with an eye on tailoring payments to needs rather than offering a standard weekly amount for everyone.

Few will be able to deny there is a need to fix the system to target support more effectively: one in six working-age claimants now say they have no additional costs relating to their disability, according to the Resolution Foundation.

For others, meanwhile, Pip doesn’t come close to covering their costs: Scope research last year found the shortfall between the average Pip award and average costs was £630 a month. And yet, years of faulty benefit testing mean campaigners will be highly concerned about whether authorities will be able to accurately work out who needs what or whether it will simply lead to reduced eligibility. With the Timms report saying Pip is “not appropriate” for those who do not incur additional costs, that is an increasingly urgent question to resolve.

Equally challenging will be Timms’s other big proposal, to introduce a “service exchange scheme” where a person would be able to choose to swap part of their financial award for a service, such as access to education or referrals into services such as health or social care.

It would in theory follow a similar model to the longrunning Motability scheme, in which some people swap the mobility component of Pip for a leased car, though how it would affect people’s choice within a service, such as hiring their own care staff, is unknown.
Crucially, any swap would be voluntary, putting Timms at direct odds with Milburn who last week said most young people should lose their right to monthly cash.

For a report that involved a mammoth consultation with more than 38,000 people and organisations, the irony is that in many ways the work has just begun. The government will now consider the review’s recommendations alongside Milburn’s and set out a response in the coming weeks, ahead of a white paper in the new year.
Related: ‘The whole process just doesn’t work’: claimants relive the agonies of Pip assessments

Downing Street will be at pains to stress this is not a competition – that both men have many points of agreements – but it will be hard to shake off the awkward position the government finds itself in, with two different sets of recommendations for one benefit.

Labour MPs who scuppered Starmer’s Pip bill last summer are unlikely to repeat the same rebellion with a popular Andy Burnham premiership. But there will be concern on the left of the party about whether Milburn’s controversial “two-tier” plan to cut benefits for young people will be given the green light.

Others will be vigilant about whether some of Timms’s more minor positive proposals – such as improving assessors’ training and introducing a digital “Tell Us Once” approach so people are not asked to provide the same information again – may get lost in all the noise.
Expect more fireworks when ministers have to decide whether any policies they do adopt will apply only to new claimants or the several million current ones too.

That Burnham is already being warned by some that adopting Timms’s ideas could increase the benefits bill, while others say it will mean hundreds of thousands losing their benefits, sums up the dilemma – and insecurity – that will define the coming months.
For a prime minister who entered office promising he would not bring in “crude cuts”, Burnham may now be asked to put his money where his mouth is.

articles.title: ‘Trapped in grief’: wife of Japanese journalist detained by Russia pleads for his release
articles.summary: Yuki Imai being held in Moscow on allegations he conducted ‘espionage’ while working for a newspaper in Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east
body: The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release.

Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east.

Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi, have denied the claims.
Related: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying

His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China.

The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war.
In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”.

“Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.”

She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.”

Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.”
Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer.

Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”.

Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.”
Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said.

The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro.
Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents.

“They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.”

articles.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
articles.summary: Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged
body: A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

The nine workers had their contracts terminated in January 2024 “in the interests of the agency” and were told in termination letters that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”. The dismissals were confirmed after a UN investigation found they might have been involved in the 7 October attacks.

The decision, which was taken by former Unrwa commissioner general Philippe Lazzarini after consultation with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, was apparently made in the hope that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work to continue in Gaza.
Critics warned at the time that the decision, on the basis of allegations rather than evidence, compromised the UN’s integrity and had the opposite effect, giving credence to unproven allegations.
The dismissals failed to prevent the Biden administration ordering a pause in funding, a measure that was echoed temporarily by other backers, leading to a financial shortfall of $450m (£340m).

“I have always said on the record that the Israeli allegations against Unrwa were the mother of all lies,” said Chris Gunness, a former Unrwa spokesperson. “Sacking the workers without any evidence confirmed their guilt unfairly, in the minds of journalists, led 16 top donors to abandon Unrwa and produced the worst financial crisis in the agency’s history, from which it may never recover.”
The Unrwa dispute tribunal that ruled in favour of one of its sacked workers, Abu Awad, described the Israeli allegations as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability”.

The tribunal also found that an internal UN investigation had not interviewed the 19 staff members initially accused by Israel of involvement in the 7 October attacks because of “safety and security” concerns.
“The allegations against the applicant and the other staff members, it seems, are therefore based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession,” the tribunal said.

It cast doubt on intercepted mobile phone conversations and messages offered by Israel as evidence, noting that one case had involved mistaken identity based on a cloned sim card, a common phenomenon in Gaza.

It also said that voice recognition claims made by Israel were dubious and some transcripts of conversations were found by UN investigators not to support claims that they proved links to Hamas or the 7 October attacks.

The allegation against Awad was that he was a “platoon commander” in Hamas’s military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, a claim he rejected. He was not alleged to have physically taken part in the 7 October attack and witness statements to the tribunal said he was on an Unrwa staff bus as normal.

The specific allegation against Awad was that he “had been instructed in a telephone call intercepted by Israeli intelligence to monitor the events of 7 October 2023, while simultaneously receiving Hamas intelligence updates related to the attacks”.
The tribunal said the Israeli security services had failed to clarify who was alleged to have made the call to Awad and in what way the mobile phone that received the call was associated with him.

Unrwa did not respond to a request for comment. Asked by the tribunal to provide evidence underpinning the dismissal of the workers, the agency cited the Israeli government as well as a report in the Times of Israel and another on the website UN Watch, a pro-Israel pressure group that has campaigned against Unrwa.

In its ruling, the tribunal said Unrwa’s claim that the cited sources had informed the decision to dismiss the workers was “open to some doubt” because all the supporting documents it had submitted were produced after the disputed decision was made on 26 January 2024.

Lazzarini, a Swiss humanitarian expert who left the commissioner general post in March, said he understood the tribunal’s finding might be appealed so he could not discuss the case in detail. In February 2024, he admitted his decision to sack the workers represented “reverse due process” in that the investigation followed the dismissal.

“My judgment, based on this going public, true or untrue, was I need to take the swiftest and boldest decision to show that as an agency we take this allegation seriously,” he said, adding that “the ability of the entire agency to continue to operate and deliver critical humanitarian assistance was at stake”.

The tribunal said it could not decide on the allegations against Awad but ruled that Unrwa had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to sack him. It awarded him a year’s pay and $5,000 for “moral damages”.

In the wake of its allegations against the sacked workers, Israel claimed that Unrwa was heavily infiltrated by Hamas and its parliament voted in 2024 to ban the agency from operating in Israel or in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The international court of justice stated in October 2025, however, that “Israel has not substantiated its allegations that a significant part of Unrwa’s employees are members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions”.
